common_name: Sterntaler Coreopsis (Fringed Golden Lance-Leaf Tickseed with Burgundy Eye)

planting.note: Direct sow, or set out spring transplants, into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Sterntaler is a German seed-strain selection of the native lance-leaf tickseed bred for a heavier bloom flush and a more compact habit than the wild species.

directions: Sterntaler carries the same lean-soil toughness as wild Coreopsis lanceolata but stays noticeably shorter and tidier, with each golden-yellow flower marked by a distinct reddish-brown eye at the base of the petals that most straight-species lanceolata lacks. The narrow ray petals have a lightly serrated, almost fringed edge that catches light differently than the smooth-edged flowers of Goldfink or the other lanceolata already in this dataset. Deadhead through the season to keep the heavy early flush going into a strong rebloom, and expect the clump to hold a neater, more upright profile than the sprawling native form even in poor, sandy soil. Divide congested crowns every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Sweet Dreams Coreopsis (Bicolor White-and-Raspberry Pink Tickseed)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring into consistently moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Sweet Dreams arose as a sterile mutation of American Dream and must be propagated vegetatively rather than grown from seed.

directions: Sweet Dreams sets it apart from both wild Coreopsis rosea and the solid rose-pink American Dream already in this dataset with a two-tone flower: each ray petal is crisp white at the tip and deepens to a rich raspberry-pink toward the yellow center disc, giving the bloom a painted, bicolor look. Because the plant is sterile and never sets seed, it channels its energy into an extended, heavy bloom from summer into fall rather than into seed production, and it spreads slowly by rhizome into a dense groundcover rather than self-sowing. Keep the soil evenly moist, since this species and its cultivars decline quickly in hot, dry conditions unlike most yellow-flowered coreopsis, and mulch in southern gardens to buffer roots from summer heat. Shear lightly after the first flush to renew a tidy shape and extend flowering.

common_name: Baby Sun Coreopsis (Dwarf Maroon-Eyed Golden Tickseed)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or set out nursery transplants after frost danger passes, into lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun; Baby Sun is a compact German seed strain (also sold as Sonnenkind) bred to stay shorter than typical grandiflora selections.

directions: Baby Sun stays notably more compact and front-of-border-scaled than most Coreopsis grandiflora selections, holding brilliant golden-yellow, two-inch daisies with a small dark maroon center just above a tidy mound of narrow foliage rather than on the taller, looser stems typical of the species. Its dwarf stature makes it a fit for rock gardens and container edges where full-size grandiflora cultivars would flop or need staking. Deadhead spent flowers regularly through the season to sustain the multi-week bloom flush from early to late summer, and expect it to be relatively short-lived in hot, humid climates like other grandiflora selections, so plan to start fresh seed or divide every two to three years.

common_name: Big Bang Star Cluster Coreopsis (Creamy White Tickseed with Cool-Weather Purple Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Star Cluster is a patented multi-species hybrid bred by Darrell Probst for the Big Bang series and, like its Full Moon and Creme Brulee series-mates already in this dataset, sets no viable seed.

directions: Star Cluster is the pale, cool-toned member of the Big Bang series in this dataset, carrying creamy white flowers around a small gold button center rather than the pale yellow of Full Moon or the deep apricot of Creme Brulee. As temperatures drop in fall and again in cool spring weather, a small but distinct deep-purple eye appears at the base of each petal, and a thin purple picotee edge can develop along the petal margins, a seasonal color shift not seen in the genus's warm-season yellows. Because the plant is sterile it never diverts energy into seed and instead blooms continuously from early summer into fall on branched stems well above the foliage. Shear the clump back by about a third after the first heavy flush to keep it full and encourage continued rebloom.

common_name: Marmalade Rudbeckia (Classic Large Golden-Orange Black-Eyed Susan)

planting.note: Direct sow, or start indoors 6-8 weeks earlier, after the last frost in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Marmalade is a long-standing seed strain distinguished from other hirta cultivars in this dataset by unusually large flowers on a shorter, stockier plant.

directions: Marmalade produces some of the largest single flowers among the older, non-hybrid rudbeckia seed strains, bright golden-orange rays up to five inches across surrounding a dark chocolate-brown center disc, on a plant that stays shorter and stockier than taller hirta selections like Indian Summer. Its heavy, oversized blooms sit close atop sturdy stems rather than on the long cutting-length stems of some other large-flowered strains, giving the plant a dense, front-loaded look in the border. It flowers from early summer through early fall, is a magnet for bees and butterflies, and self-seeds readily, often returning informally for a second or third season in beds where it's allowed to drop seed undisturbed. Deadhead selectively to extend bloom, or leave the last flush of seed heads standing for finches in winter.

common_name: Chim Chiminee Rudbeckia (Quilled Autumn-Toned Black-Eyed Susan)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6 weeks before the last frost with gentle bottom heat, or direct sow after frost danger passes, in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Chim Chiminee is a novelty strain grown for its narrow, quilled petals rather than the flat rays typical of most hirta cultivars.

directions: Chim Chiminee is grown for its distinctive quilled, tubular petals rather than the flat, spoon-shaped rays of standard black-eyed Susans, giving each large bloom a shaggy, spidery texture unlike any other rudbeckia already cataloged here. Flowers open in a mix of gold, burnt orange, and chocolate-bronze on a single plant, since the strain segregates for color rather than breeding true to one shade, so a packet of seed yields a naturalistic range of autumnal tones. It flowers from midsummer straight through to frost on tall, branching stems well suited to cutting, and while it only reliably overwinters as a perennial in zones 9-10, it self-sows freely elsewhere and often returns informally the following year. Stake in windy sites, since the tall stems and large flower heads can lean in exposed locations.

common_name: Tiger Eye Gold Rudbeckia (Mildew-Resistant F1 Semi-Double Black-Eyed Susan)

planting.note: Set out nursery transplants after the last frost into average to mildly alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Tiger Eye Gold is a patented F1 hybrid bred for uniform, mildew-resistant growth rather than an open-pollinated seed strain.

directions: Tiger Eye Gold bears large, semi-double, glowing orange-gold flowers around a dark brown button center, a fuller, ruffled bloom form distinct from the mostly single flowers of other hirta cultivars in this dataset. Bred as an F1 hybrid for landscape uniformity, it grows into an unusually even, well-branched mound and shows noticeably better resistance to powdery mildew than older open-pollinated black-eyed Susan strains, an important trait through humid late summers. Unlike many hirta selections grown strictly as annuals, it is hardy enough to persist as a garden perennial through zone 3, blooming heavily from midsummer to frost. Deadhead to prolong bloom, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.
